    26	  // an Int head) insert via the shared applyCmp dispatch — the exact ltIF/ltFI
    27	  // bridges (float.k) + the bool->int promotion (bool.k), so mixed sorts match
    28	  // CPython bit-exactly. X goes before Y iff not (Y < X) — the same tie rule as
    29	  // insVS's X <=Int Y, so equal keys keep first-seen order (stable insertion
    30	  // from the right). str-vs-numeric has no applyCmp leg and stays stuck
    31	  // (CPython TypeError).
    32	  syntax ValSeq ::= insVSn(Val, ValSeq) [function]
    33	  rule sortVS(vCons(X:Val, R:ValSeq)) => insVSn(X, sortVS(R))
    34	       requires isFloat(X) orBool isBool(X) [concrete]
    35	  rule insVS(X:Int, vCons(Y:Val, R:ValSeq)) => vCons(X, vCons(Y, R))
    36	       requires (isFloat(Y) orBool isBool(Y)) andBool notBool applyCmp("<", Y, X) [concrete]
    37	  rule insVS(X:Int, vCons(Y:Val, R:ValSeq)) => vCons(Y, insVS(X, R))
    38	       requires (isFloat(Y) orBool isBool(Y)) andBool applyCmp("<", Y, X) [concrete]
    39	  rule insVSn(X:Val, .ValSeq) => vCons(X, .ValSeq) [concrete]
    40	  rule insVSn(X:Val, vCons(Y:Val, R:ValSeq)) => vCons(X, vCons(Y, R))
    41	       requires notBool applyCmp("<", Y, X) [concrete]
    42	  rule insVSn(X:Val, vCons(Y:Val, R:ValSeq)) => vCons(Y, insVSn(X, R))
    43	       requires applyCmp("<", Y, X) [concrete]

    45	  syntax ValSeq ::= insVSs(IntSeq, ValSeq) [function]
    46	  rule sortVS(vCons(str(CS:IntSeq), R:ValSeq)) => insVSs(CS, sortVS(R)) [concrete]
    47	  rule insVSs(A:IntSeq, .ValSeq) => vCons(str(A), .ValSeq) [concrete]
    48	  rule insVSs(A:IntSeq, vCons(str(B:IntSeq), R:ValSeq)) => vCons(str(A), vCons(str(B), R))
    49	       requires strLt(A, B) orBool A ==K B [concrete]
    50	  rule insVSs(A:IntSeq, vCons(str(B:IntSeq), R:ValSeq)) => vCons(str(B), insVSs(A, R))
    51	       requires notBool (strLt(A, B) orBool A ==K B) [concrete]
    52	
    53	  // sorted(list) constructs a NEW object: k-cell pre-dispatch (beats the [owise]
    54	  // applyBuiltin routing in call.k) so the result allocates.
    55	  rule <k> #applyK(toCall(builtinV("sorted")), (list(VS:ValSeq), .Vals))
    56	        => #alloc(list(sortVS(VS))) ... </k>
    57	
    58	  // mutator: xs.sort() — the in-place heap write over the same trusted sortVS
    59	  rule <k> #applyK(toCall(boundMethodV(ref(H:Int), "sort")), .Vals) => noneV ... </k>
    60	       <heap> ... H |-> list(VS:ValSeq => sortVS(VS)) ... </heap>
    61	       [priority(40)]
    62	
    63	  // ==== keyed / reversed sorted() (WP2) =====================================
    64	  // sortKeyVS(VS, KV): the stable ascending sort of VS by the key value KV
    65	  // (a closure/builtin/type — anything callable). OPAQUE here; the concrete
    66	  // leg (MPY-CONCRETE, llvm only) computes keys by REAL calls and stable-
    67	  // inserts, at priority(40) over these.
    68	  syntax ValSeq ::= sortKeyVS(ValSeq, Val) [function, total, symbol(sortKeyVS), no-evaluators]
    69	
    70	  syntax ValSeq ::= revVS(ValSeq) [function, total]
    71	                  | revVSAcc(ValSeq, ValSeq) [function, total]
    72	  rule revVS(S:ValSeq) => revVSAcc(S, .ValSeq)
    73	  rule revVSAcc(.ValSeq, A:ValSeq) => A
    74	  rule revVSAcc(vCons(V:Val, R:ValSeq), A:ValSeq) => revVSAcc(R, vCons(V, A))
    75	
    76	  syntax ValSeq ::= condRev(ValSeq, Bool) [function, total]
    77	  rule condRev(S:ValSeq, false) => S
    78	  rule condRev(S:ValSeq, true)  => revVS(S)
    79	
    80	  rule <k> #applyK(toCall(builtinV("sorted")), (list(VS:ValSeq), kwV("key", KV:Val), .Vals))
    81	        => #alloc(list(sortKeyVS(VS, KV))) ... </k>
    82	  rule <k> #applyK(toCall(builtinV("sorted")), (list(VS:ValSeq), kwV("key", KV:Val), kwV("reverse", RB:Bool), .Vals))
    83	        => #alloc(list(condRev(sortKeyVS(VS, KV), RB))) ... </k>
    84	  rule <k> #applyK(toCall(builtinV("sorted")), (list(VS:ValSeq), kwV("reverse", RB:Bool), .Vals))
    85	        => #alloc(list(condRev(sortVS(VS), RB))) ... </k>
    86	
    87	  // Indexing the opaque sorted list: `valSeqAt(sortVS(VS), I)` is DEFINED because valSeqAt is
    88	  // [total] (subscript.k) — it stays an abstract total value for a symbolic sort and reduces
    89	  // over the concrete sort for krun. No separate sortedAt indirection is needed; wrappers write
    90	  // their postcondition directly as valSeqAt(sortVS(VS), …).

     3	module MPY-SUBSCRIPT

     5	
     6	  // ==== positional access + negative-index normalization (used only here) ===

     8	  // a trusted sort's sortVS(VS)) or OOB it stays an abstract total value — so indexing the
     9	  // opaque sorted list is DEFINED (no undischarged #Ceil), matching the old semantics' total
    10	  // atK. K trusts the [total] annotation; valid programs index in-bounds.
    11	  syntax Val ::= valSeqAt(ValSeq, Int) [function, total]
    12	  rule valSeqAt(vCons(V:Val, _:ValSeq), 0)     => V
    13	  rule valSeqAt(vCons(_:Val, S:ValSeq), I:Int) => valSeqAt(S, I -Int 1)
    14	       requires I >Int 0
    15	
    16	  syntax Int ::= intSeqAt(IntSeq, Int) [function]
    17	  rule intSeqAt(iCons(C:Int, _:IntSeq), 0)     => C
    18	  rule intSeqAt(iCons(_:Int, S:IntSeq), I:Int) => intSeqAt(S, I -Int 1)
    19	       requires I >Int 0
    20	
    21	  syntax Int ::= normIdx(Int, Int) [function, total]
    22	  rule normIdx(I:Int, LEN:Int) => I +Int LEN requires I  <Int 0
    23	  rule normIdx(I:Int, _:Int)   => I          requires I >=Int 0
    24	
    25	  // ==== Subscript: indexing obj[i] (list / tuple / str) =====================
    26	  // contexts (not strict attrs): the Index slot's Slice alternative must never heat
    27	  context Subscript(HOLE, _)
    28	  context Subscript(_:Val, HOLE:Expr)
    29	
    30	  // heap-object deref (covers both the index and slice forms via the Index slot)
    31	  rule <k> Subscript(ref(H:Int), IX:Index) => Subscript(V, IX) ... </k>
    32	       <heap> ... H |-> V:Val ... </heap>
    33	       [priority(40)]
    34	
    35	  rule <k> Subscript(OBJ:Val, I:Int) => applyIndex(OBJ, I) ... </k>
    36	
    37	  syntax Val ::= applyIndex(Val, Int) [function]
    38	  rule applyIndex(list(VS:ValSeq),  I:Int) => valSeqAt(VS, normIdx(I, vsLen(VS)))
    39	  rule applyIndex(tuple(VS:ValSeq), I:Int) => valSeqAt(VS, normIdx(I, vsLen(VS)))
    40	  rule applyIndex(str(IS:IntSeq),   I:Int)
    41	    => str(iCons(intSeqAt(IS, normIdx(I, isLen(IS))), .IntSeq))
    42	
    43	  // ==== Slice: obj[lo:hi:step] (list / str) — CPython slice.indices ==========
    44	  syntax KItem ::= #evalB(Bound) | "#toSome"
    45	                 | #slLo(Val, Bound, Bound)
    46	                 | #slHi(Val, OptInt, Bound)
    47	                 | #slStep(Val, OptInt, OptInt)
    48	
    49	  syntax OptInt ::= "noB" | someB(Int)

    51	  rule <k> #evalB(E:Expr)   => E ~> #toSome ... </k>
    52	  rule <k> I:Int ~> #toSome => someB(I) ... </k>
    53	
    54	  rule <k> Subscript(OBJ:Val, Slice(LO:Bound, HI:Bound, ST:Bound)) => #evalB(LO) ~> #slLo(OBJ, HI, ST) ... </k>
    55	  rule <k> LO:OptInt ~> #slLo(OBJ:Val, HI:Bound, ST:Bound)   => #evalB(HI) ~> #slHi(OBJ, LO, ST) ... </k>
    56	  rule <k> HI:OptInt ~> #slHi(OBJ:Val, LO:OptInt, ST:Bound)  => #evalB(ST) ~> #slStep(OBJ, LO, HI) ... </k>
    57	  // a list slice constructs a NEW object; a str slice stays a value
    58	  rule <k> ST:OptInt ~> #slStep(list(VS:ValSeq), LO:OptInt, HI:OptInt)

    63	  syntax Val ::= doSlice(Val, OptInt, OptInt, OptInt) [function]
    64	  rule doSlice(list(VS:ValSeq), LO:OptInt, HI:OptInt, ST:OptInt)
    65	    => list(buildVS(VS, slStart(LO, ST, vsLen(VS)), slStop(HI, ST, vsLen(VS)), slStep(ST)))
    66	  rule doSlice(tuple(VS:ValSeq), LO:OptInt, HI:OptInt, ST:OptInt)
    67	    => tuple(buildVS(VS, slStart(LO, ST, vsLen(VS)), slStop(HI, ST, vsLen(VS)), slStep(ST)))

    69	    => str(buildIS(IS, slStart(LO, ST, isLen(IS)), slStop(HI, ST, isLen(IS)), slStep(ST)))

    71	  // ==== slice.indices: step / start / stop / clamp ==========================
    72	  syntax Int ::= slStep(OptInt) [function, total]

    74	  rule slStep(someB(S:Int)) => S

requires "reference-semantics/semantics.k"

module REVIEWER-PINNING
  imports MPY

  syntax Stmts ::= "REVIEWED-PROGRAM-BODY" [macro]
  rule REVIEWED-PROGRAM-BODY
    => Assign(Name("strongest"), Str(""))
       Assign(Name("best_strength"), NoneVal)
       Assign(Name("extension"), Str(""))
       Assign(Name("character"), Str(""))
       For(
         Name("extension"),
         Name("extensions"),
         Assign(Name("strength"), Int(0))
         For(
           Name("character"),
           Name("extension"),
           If(
             Call(Attribute(Name("character"), "isupper"), .Exprs),
             AugAssign(Name("strength"), "+", Int(1)) .Stmts,
             If(
               Call(Attribute(Name("character"), "islower"), .Exprs),
               AugAssign(Name("strength"), "-", Int(1)) .Stmts,
               .Stmts
             ) .Stmts
           ) .Stmts
         )
         If(
           BoolOp(
             "or",
             Compare(Name("best_strength"), CmpOp("is", NoneVal)),
             Compare(Name("strength"), CmpOp(">", Name("best_strength"))),
             .Exprs
           ),
           Assign(Name("strongest"), Name("extension"))
           Assign(Name("best_strength"), Name("strength"))
           .Stmts,
           .Stmts
         )
         .Stmts
       )
       Return(
         BinOp(
           "+",
           BinOp("+", Name("class_name"), Str(".")),
           Name("strongest")
         )
       )
       .Stmts
endmodule

## Authority, isolation, and output

This benchmark prompt controls the final `PASS` / `CONCERNS` / `FAIL` mapping
when generic Kit status terminology is less specific. In particular, a Kit
`SOUND-BUT-LIMITED` finding caused by materially narrowing the HumanEval
source-contract domain is `FAIL / NOT_LEGIT`, not `CONCERNS / LEGIT`.

Campaign amendment v2 (2026-07-30) refines that mapping with two exceptions;
neither weakens any other rule:

1. A __documented supplied-model representation gap__ maps to
   `CONCERNS / LEGIT` when ALL of the following hold: the restriction
   originates in the supplied read-only reference semantics rather than the
   candidate (a value class, identification, encoding, or behavior the fixed
   model cannot represent); the theorem covers every input the fixed model
   does represent, with no additional narrowing of the candidate's own
   making; the boundary is recorded explicitly in the trust ledger with a
   concrete divergence witness; and the submitted Python program is faithful
   to the intended CPython behavior on the gap (the divergence is
   model-vs-CPython, not program-vs-canonical). A candidate-caused
   narrowing, an undocumented gap, or a program that itself diverges from
   canonical on model-representable inputs remains `FAIL / NOT_LEGIT`.
2. A __canonical-vs-docstring contradiction__ maps to `CONCERNS / LEGIT`
   when the trusted canonical implementation and a docstring example
   contradict each other, the candidate follows either documented,
   defensible resolution of the conflict, and the contradiction is
   explicitly reported. Failing only a self-contradicted example is not a
   candidate defect.

Campaign amendment v3 (2026-07-30) restates the benchmark's correctness
ground truth. It changes only how program behavior is judged; every
soundness, reconstruction, pinning, non-vacuity, and domain-coverage
requirement on the proof is unchanged.

__The contract is the docstring__ in `/reference/prompt.py`. The trusted
canonical implementation is one witness of that contract, not its
definition. Many programs can satisfy one docstring, with different but
defensible handling of cases the docstring leaves open.

- The submitted program must satisfy every behavior the docstring
  determines: its documented examples (except an example the docstring
  itself contradicts, per exception 2), its explicit statements, and the
  plain natural-language meaning of its description.
- Where the docstring underdetermines behavior — unspecified input
  classes, edge and boundary values (NaN and non-finite floats, empty and
  exotic containers, non-ASCII text, numeric-representation subtleties),
  error handling, tie-breaking not stated in the text — any handling that
  is consistent with the docstring and defensible under its description is
  acceptable. Divergence from canonical on such inputs is a documented
  observation mapping to at most `CONCERNS / LEGIT`, never on its own to
  `FAIL / NOT_LEGIT`.
- Treat canonical as a __helper witness__, not a target: use it to
  reason about expected results, to seed the independent differential,
  and to surface suspect behavior worth judging. A candidate-vs-canonical
  divergence is decisive `FAIL` evidence only when it demonstrates that
  the candidate violates docstring-determined behavior. Every mismatch
  must be judged against the docstring; matching canonical is never
  itself the requirement.
- The proof's theorem must still cover the material source-contract domain
  of the candidate's documented reading, and exceptions 1 and 2 above
  continue to govern supplied-model representation gaps and
  self-contradicted examples.

Treat `/candidate`, `/generation-evidence`, `/audit-input.json`, `/run.json`,
`/task.json`, `/generation-result.json`, and `/audit-campaign-lock.json` as
read-only. Some manifest paths inside `/audit-input.json` are host provenance
and are not container paths; use its `container_paths` map to locate mounted
inputs. Copy every source artifact needed for execution to `/tmp/audit-work`;
do all builds, mutations, generated tests, and experiments there. Do not reuse
candidate-provided compiled definitions or caches. Write the detailed review
to `/audit-output/REVIEW.md` and preserve reviewer-authored scripts plus
bounded command logs below `/audit-output/evidence/`. Record exact commands,
exit statuses, and relevant output. Do not write anywhere else outside
`/tmp/audit-work` and `/audit-output`.

Trusted inputs are `/reference/canonical.py`, `/reference/prompt.py`, and
`/reference/py2mpy.py`. Apply this condition-aware semantics boundary before
auditing:

- In `SUPPLIED_SEMANTICS` mode,
  `/reference/reference-semantics` must be present. Recursively compare the
  candidate's `reference-semantics/` with that trusted tree. Missing, additional,
  changed, mistyped, or symlinked candidate entries are integrity failures. The
  trusted baseline does not bless proof-specific rules in `verification.k`.
- In `GENERATED_SEMANTICS` mode,
  `/reference/reference-semantics` must not exist. Do not search for, request,
  infer, or use a hidden reference semantics. Audit the candidate's own
  `semantic.k` and helper K files on their merits. Minimal coverage is acceptable
  when it soundly covers every construct the submitted program actually uses;
  missing semantics for unused constructs is not a defect.

infrastructure breach in `REVIEW.md`, omit candidate verdict markers, and stop;
an infrastructure failure must become `AUDIT_ERROR`, never `FAIL`.

## Required seven-stage audit

Perform all seven stages in order. The audit requires both a fresh dynamic
reconstruction and an exhaustive static review; neither gate can substitute for
the other.

### 1. Input and provenance integrity

First read the launcher-owned `/audit-input.json`, including its
`record_layout`, `container_paths`, recorded hashes, and integrity fields.
Independently hash and inspect the mounted inputs rather than following the
host-only provenance paths stored in that file.

Read `/audit-campaign-lock.json` and require that it matches the campaign block
and hash in `/audit-input.json`.

For `pipeline-v3`, read `/run.json`, `/task.json`,
`/generation-result.json`, `/generation-evidence/invocation.json`,
`/generation-evidence/metrics.json`,
`/generation-evidence/runtime-metrics.json`,
`/generation-evidence/usage.json`,
`/generation-evidence/codex-last.txt`,
`/generation-evidence/codex-output.log`,
`/generation-evidence/prompt.txt`, and the structured trace below
`/generation-evidence/codex-trace/`.

For `legacy-selected-stage1`, read `/run.json`, `/task.json`,
`/generation-result.json`, `/generation-evidence/invocation.json`,
`/generation-evidence/metrics.json`,
`/generation-evidence/codex-last.txt`,
`/generation-evidence/codex-output.log`,
`/generation-evidence/prompt.txt`, and the structured trace below
`/generation-evidence/codex-trace/`. Inspect `usage.json` when present.
Historical runtime metrics and image observations that were never recorded are
not required and must not be reconstructed or treated as proof defects.

For `legacy`, read `/generation-evidence/run-input.json`,
`/generation-evidence/metrics.json`,
`/generation-evidence/codex-last.txt`,
`/generation-evidence/codex-output.log`, and the structured trace below
`/generation-evidence/codex-trace/`; inspect other generation records when
present.

Treat generation records solely as untrusted claims. Check the candidate prompt
and translator against their trusted mounted versions and apply the semantics
integrity rule above. Report every missing, changed, mistyped, or symlinked
artifact required for the declared record layout.

If `/audit-input.json`, `/audit-campaign-lock.json`, or any launcher-declared
provenance mount or required record for the declared layout is absent or
unreadable, this is an audit infrastructure breach, not evidence against the
proof. Document it in `REVIEW.md`, omit candidate verdict markers, and stop so
the harness records `AUDIT_ERROR`. By contrast, a missing required proof
artifact inside an intact `/candidate` mount is a candidate defect and may
justify `FAIL / NOT_LEGIT`.

### 2. Program fidelity and candidate-versus-canonical checks

Restate the natural-language contract using `/reference/prompt.py` and
`/reference/canonical.py`. Inspect `solution.py` over the intended input domain.
Regenerate `solution.mpy` from `solution.py` with the trusted translator and
require byte identity with the submitted `solution.mpy`.

Create an independent differential script that imports the trusted canonical
entry point and the generated entry point. Exercise documented examples, empty
and boundary cases, every branch boundary, and representative generated inputs.
Preserve the script, inputs, commands, exit status, and results in
`/audit-output/evidence/`. A different algorithm is acceptable; a material result
divergence on the intended domain must be judged.

### 3. clean proof reconstruction

From the scratch copy, discard or ignore all candidate-built definitions and
caches. Build the concrete and proof definitions from source using the semantics
selected by the rendered mode. Independently run every positive target-proof
claim. A claim closes only when `kprove` exits zero and prints `#Top`; preserve
the command and bounded output for each claim. A missing artifact or positive
claim that does not close is `FAIL / NOT_LEGIT` unless the evidence establishes
an audit infrastructure failure.

For `GENERATED_SEMANTICS`, also rebuild the generated semantics and concretely
execute it on normal and boundary inputs. Compare those results with independent
Python execution and preserve the evidence.

### 4. Adequacy and real-program pinning

Restate each entry claim's precondition and postcondition in plain language.
Verify that the `<k>` cell executes the actual submitted `solution.mpy` program,
that every helper or loop claim matches real control flow, and that the returned
value is constrained to the intended result rather than a free variable,
tautology, or one-way implication where equivalence is required. Exhibit at
least one state satisfying every entry precondition. Substitute concrete
satisfying inputs into the claimed result and compare it with both Python
implementations.

The claim need not literally read or begin with the complete `solution.mpy`
module. It pins the submitted program when trusted regeneration plus a
mechanical constructor-level comparison shows that the executed claim term is
the same function binding and body, allowing only demonstrated semantically
inert normalization such as omitted typing-only imports or syntax macros that
expand to that term. Fixed semantics must still execute every material operation
and control effect. Treat lack of automatic source-to-proof regeneration as an
artifact-maintenance observation, not a proof failure for the immutable
candidate. A body-sensitivity mutation must change the program term actually
executed by the claim; changing only an external source file while leaving that
term unchanged does not test the theorem's dependence on its body.

### 5. rule-by-rule static soundness review

Create an exhaustive rule inventory for `semantic.k`, generated helper K files,
and `verification.k` as applicable. Enumerate every local syntax declaration,
function, `total` or `functional` declaration, opaque symbol, priority rule,
ordinary semantic rule, and simplification rule. Map every syntactic construct
used by `solution.mpy` to its declaration and rules. Check configuration and
cells, evaluation order and control flow, state changes and allocation, calls
and returns, guards, overlaps, priorities, totality, and simplifications.

Decide for every inventoried rule whether it follows from the selected semantics
level, the real program behavior, and ordinary mathematics. Every unsoundness
claim must include a concrete or symbolic false conclusion witness that the rule
can enable on the intended input domain. Without such a witness, do not label the
rule unsound; state the narrower evidence gap instead. Reject rules that encode
the task's answer, replace a property-bearing computation with an unconstrained
oracle, bypass real execution, silently fabricate results for unmodeled used
constructs, or otherwise make a false claim provable. Distinguish an acceptable
low-level trust boundary from a smuggled correctness conclusion.

### 6. Fresh non-vacuity test

Inspect any candidate `spec-vacuity.k` only as untrusted evidence. In scratch,
create a fresh, meaningful false mutation that changes a result-constraining
obligation and is demonstrably false for at least one satisfying input. Require
the mutation to build successfully and the proof to fail because of the expected
unmet obligation. A parser error, missing import, timeout, unrelated crash, or
mutation that was never reachable is not non-vacuity evidence. Preserve the
mutation and its build/proof logs.

### 7. proven versus assumed accounting

State precisely what the successful reachability proof establishes. List every
trusted primitive, opaque symbol, empirical bridge, and informal argument.
Explain why each boundary is acceptable, concerning, or illegitimate. Do not
accept `PROOF.md`, generated traces, or differential testing as a substitute for
the K proof; differential evidence may support only the bridge it actually
tests.

## Decision boundary

- `PASS / LEGIT`: the reconstructed proof is sound, result-constraining, and
  pins the real generated program, with no material adequacy gap.

+# Independent adversarial review: 153-Strongest-Extension
+
+## Overall determination
+
+The candidate contains a legitimate, non-vacuous partial-correctness proof of
+the submitted program under the supplied K model. The proof is unbounded over
+all finite strings and all finite lists of strings representable as the model's
+`IntSeq`/`ValSeq` values, pins the exact translated function body, and constrains
+the returned string to the first extension with maximal score.
+
+The result is `CONCERNS / LEGIT`, rather than `PASS / LEGIT`, because the
+read-only supplied semantics defines upper- and lower-case characters as ASCII
+code-point ranges. CPython's predicates are Unicode-aware. The candidate did
+not introduce this restriction, proves every string/list value admitted by the
+fixed model, explicitly records the boundary and the `Ω` witness in
+`/candidate/PROOF.md:174`, and its Python source behaves correctly under
+CPython on that witness. This is the documented supplied-model behavior gap
+covered by campaign amendment v2.
+
+All execution and mutation work used the clean scratch tree
+`/tmp/audit-work/153-strongest-extension`. Candidate caches and compiled
+definitions were not copied or used. Reviewer-authored sources and command
+logs are in [`evidence/`](/audit-output/evidence).
+
+## 1. Input and provenance integrity
+
+`/audit-input.json` declares `pipeline-v3`, problem
+`153-Strongest-Extension`, condition `kit-semantics`,
+`SUPPLIED_SEMANTICS`, and a required reference-semantics mount. The mount
+`/reference/reference-semantics` is present, so the rendered mode and trusted
+mount agree.
+
+I read all launcher-required records for this layout: `/run.json`,
+`/task.json`, `/generation-result.json`, the invocation, generation/runtime
+metrics, usage, last message, output log, generation prompt, and the complete
+structured trace. The single JSONL trace contains 1,039 valid records:
+1 session record, 317 event messages, 715 response items, 2 world states,
+3 turn contexts, and 1 compaction record. These records were treated only as
+untrusted history.
+
+The independent provenance checker in
+[`provenance_check.py`](/audit-output/evidence/provenance_check.py) establishes:
+
+- the campaign-lock JSON equals the campaign block and its SHA-256 is
+  `053ed73c...dadd01`, exactly the recorded value;
+- every required pipeline-v3 record is readable, and every individually
+  recorded SHA-256 for the run, task, result, invocation, metrics, runtime
+  metrics, usage, last message, output log, generation prompt, canonical,
+  trusted prompt, and translator matches the mounted bytes;
+- the direct trace-file hash matches the hash in `generation-result.json`;
+- candidate `prompt.py` and `py2mpy.py` are byte-identical to their trusted
+  mounts;
+- a recursive entry-type and per-file-content comparison of the candidate and
+  trusted `reference-semantics/` trees is identical across all 26 entries;
+- there are no symlinks below the candidate, reference, or generation-evidence
+  mounts; and
+- all required source proof artifacts are regular files.
+
+The checker also records independent reviewer tree manifests and the
+launcher-recorded aggregate hashes without treating either hashing convention
+as a substitute for the direct recursive comparison. Full command, hashes,
+trace counts, and exit status 0 are in
+[`01_provenance.log`](/audit-output/evidence/01_provenance.log). There is no
+provenance or audit-infrastructure breach.
+
+## 2. Program fidelity and candidate-versus-canonical checks
+
+### Contract
+
+The trusted docstring says to score each extension name as the number of
+uppercase letters minus the number of lowercase letters, select the strongest,
+choose the first on a tie, and return
+`ClassName.StrongestExtensionName`. Both documented examples determine those
+behaviors. It does not specify what to do with an empty extension list.
+
+The candidate source at `/candidate/solution.py:1`:
+
+- initializes no winner with `best_strength = None`, which correctly permits
+  a first extension with a negative score;
+- counts each one-character iteration using `isupper()` and, otherwise,
+  `islower()`;
+- updates only on strict `>`, preserving the first extension on ties; and
+- returns the required dotted concatenation.
+
+For a single Python character, the canonical test
+`isalpha() and isupper()/islower()` and the candidate's direct case predicates
+produce the same contribution. The different algorithm is therefore faithful.
+On an empty list, the candidate returns `class_name + "."` while canonical
+raises `IndexError`; this input is underdetermined by the docstring, and the
+candidate's total extension is defensible.
+
+Running the trusted `/reference/py2mpy.py` on the candidate Python source
+produced a byte-for-byte identical `solution.mpy`; see
+[`02_translation_identity.log`](/audit-output/evidence/02_translation_identity.log).
+
+The independent differential program
+[`independent_differential.py`](/audit-output/evidence/independent_differential.py)
+loaded the trusted canonical and candidate entry points. It exercised both
+documented examples, empty strings, an empty list, negative scores, all three
+case categories, greater/equal/less update boundaries, Unicode, and 10,000
+deterministically generated nonempty cases. There were zero candidate/canonical
+or candidate/doc-oracle mismatches on the 10,015 nonempty cases. The empty-list
+difference was observed and classified as underdetermined.
+
+The same test provides the concrete model-gap witness:
+`("Gap", ["", "Ω"])`. CPython candidate and canonical both return
+`"Gap.Ω"`; the supplied model's ASCII score makes the two extensions tie and
+selects `"Gap."`. Inputs, outputs, and exit status 0 are preserved in
+[`02_independent_differential.log`](/audit-output/evidence/02_independent_differential.log).
+

+`*-kompiled` directories, archive, log, or caches. Tool versions are recorded

+bridges for the outer connection, and the final target definition. All builds

`total`, 26 `no-evaluators`, 28 `symbol`, 51 `priority`, 29 `owise`, 12
`simplification`, 62 `concrete`, 3 `preserves-definedness`, 7 `macro`, and
1 `macro-rec`. The unimported mutation/spec-vacuity artifacts have no path
into the successful theorem.

### Used-construct coverage

Every constructor in the submitted `solution.mpy` has both a syntax
declaration and a material execution path:

| Program construct | Supplied declaration/execution rules |
|---|---|
| `Module`, `FuncDef`, `Params` | `semantics/syntax.k`; `core.k` `#loadAll`; `functions.k` closure creation |
| `Call`, arguments, return | `call.k` callee and left-to-right argument machinery, closure frame rules; `functions.k` return/pop |
| `Name`, `Int`, `Str`, `NoneVal` | `core.k` lookup and literal rules |
| `Assign`, `AugAssign` | `controls.k` local writes and rewrite through `BinOp` |
| `For`, list iteration, string iteration | `controls.k` `#loop/#loopStep`; `list.k` and `str.k` `#iterNext`; target binding rules |
| `If` | `controls.k` truth evaluation and branch selection |
| short-circuit `or` | `bool.k` contexts and truthy/falsey continuation rules |
| `is`, integer `>`, integer `+/-` | `operators.k` and `int.k` |
| attribute method calls | `call.k`/attribute dispatch; `methods.k` `isupper` and `islower` |
| string `+` | `operators.k` dispatch and `str.k` `seqConcat` |

The fixed configuration accounts for `<k>`, environment/scopes, allocation
and heap, call stack, return, exception, and exit status. Call frames and local
writes preserve evaluation order and state. The program performs no mutable
container update; list/string inputs are iterated, and string concatenation
constructs the returned value.

### Supplied rules

The candidate's entire `reference-semantics/` is byte- and type-identical to
the trusted read-only tree. Its many rule families unrelated to this program
(floats, dicts, sets, sorting, comprehensions, slicing, and other builtins) are
inert here. The used fixed rules have ordinary deterministic roles described
above. Their overlaps are resolved by their fixed sorts, guards, `owise`, and
priorities.

The one material model limitation is in `semantics/methods.k`: `isUpperC`
recognizes 65--90 and `isLowerC` recognizes 97--122. This is internally
consistent with the theorem's `charStrength`; it is not CPython's Unicode
classification. A bridge-free exact-program claim under the trusted semantics
for `("Gap", ["", "Ω"])` proves the fixed result `"Gap."`, independently
confirming the divergence:

- [`reviewer-pinning.k`](/audit-output/evidence/reviewer-pinning.k)
- [`model_gap_spec.k`](/audit-output/evidence/model_gap_spec.k)
- [`05_build_reviewer_pinning.log`](/audit-output/evidence/05_build_reviewer_pinning.log)
- [`05_prove_model_gap.log`](/audit-output/evidence/05_prove_model_gap.log)

### Candidate definitions and rules

The three `INNER-BODY`, `OUTER-BODY`, and `STRONGEST-BODY` rules are macros:
they expand to the exact translated syntax and add no alternate execution
semantics.

The mathematical helpers are structural computations, not answer axioms:

- `charStrength` has three disjoint and exhaustive guarded ASCII cases;
  `extensionStrength` and `lastCharacter` recurse on a strictly smaller
  `IntSeq`.
- `isStringVal` and `allStrings` are exact constructor predicates.
- `bestCodes` and `bestScore` split on strict `>` versus its Boolean negation,
  descend the `ValSeq`, and retain the earlier winner on equality.
- `lastExtension`, `lastStrength`, and `lastCharacterAcross` exactly summarize
  the source locals and descend the tail.
- `expectedResult` adds the dot and, for nonempty input, uses the first
  extension as the initial winner and score.

The guarded projection layer deserves special scrutiny. `Str` has the sole
constructor `str(IntSeq)` in the fixed model. `projectStrTotal` and
`codesProject` expose that constructor only when `isStringVal` is true;
`codesProject` remains opaque outside that domain. Every result-bearing use is
guarded by `isStringVal` or `allStrings`. The forward/reverse projection
simplifiers therefore express the fixed datatype identity rather than
fabricating a string. As an independent negative check, the false claim that
projecting concrete `"A"` yields `""` built, reached a stuck state, and exited
1 in [`05_projection_opposite.log`](/audit-output/evidence/05_projection_opposite.log).
The projection connection's own `#Top` is consequently supported by static
datatype analysis and this negative probe, not accepted solely because its
simplifier makes the positive claim trivial.

There are three operational bridge rules:

1. The priority-40 yield rule is the fixed `#iterYield/#loopStep` transition
   with a statically typed string projection. Its universal connection claim
   is proved in `VERIFICATION-BASE`, before this rule is imported.
2. The priority-30 inner-loop rule summarizes exactly the submitted inner body
   in the exact closed seven-binding frame. Its universal connection claim is
   also proved before import.
3. The priority-20 outer-loop rule summarizes exactly the submitted outer
   body and five changed locals under `allStrings`. Its connection claim is
   proved after importing only the already-connected yield/inner rules and
   before importing the outer bridge itself.

This dependency order avoids a bridge proving its own connection. The bridge
left sides fix the real loop target and body; arbitrary following computation
is framed by `...`. Fresh continuation-sensitive claims put an observable
assignment after an inner loop and obtain the same final state with the fixed
rules and with the bridge:

- [`fixed_continuation_spec.k`](/audit-output/evidence/fixed_continuation_spec.k)
- [`bridge_continuation_spec.k`](/audit-output/evidence/bridge_continuation_spec.k)
- [`05_fixed_continuation.log`](/audit-output/evidence/05_fixed_continuation.log)
- [`05_bridge_continuation.log`](/audit-output/evidence/05_bridge_continuation.log)

The outer bridge requires an integer best score, but this does not narrow the
nonempty entry domain: the first iteration executes through the fixed
semantics while `best_strength` is `None`, installs the first integer score,
and only then can the bridge summarize an arbitrary tail. The empty entry has
its own theorem. `allStrings` is exactly the docstring's extension-name input
class, not a finite-size bound or a candidate-created restriction. Class
strings, first strings, tails, and character sequences all remain symbolic and
unbounded in finite length.

No inventoried candidate rule bypasses the function call, asserts the task
answer, substitutes a different program, or introduces an unconstrained
result oracle. I found no rule capable of enabling a false conclusion on the
claimed fixed-model domain. Accordingly, there is no unsoundness accusation
for which a false-conclusion witness is being withheld.

## 6. Fresh non-vacuity test

I ignored the candidate's `spec-vacuity.k` as proof of this gate and wrote the
fresh claim
[`reviewer-vacuity.k`](/audit-output/evidence/reviewer-vacuity.k). It loads the
exact submitted function on the satisfying concrete input
`Strongest_Extension("C", ["a", "B"])`, but deliberately requires the wrong
winner `"C.a"` instead of the actual `"C.B"`.

The dry run generated the proof command and exited 0, establishing that the
mutation parsed and built:
[`06_vacuity_dry_run.log`](/audit-output/evidence/06_vacuity_dry_run.log).
The real proof executed the program, reported `WarnStuckClaimState`, and exited
1:
[`06_vacuity_proof.log`](/audit-output/evidence/06_vacuity_proof.log). This is
the expected unmet result obligation, not a parser error, timeout, missing
import, or unreachable mutation. The theorem is non-vacuous.

## 7. Proven-versus-assumed accounting

### What the reachability proof establishes

Under the supplied semantics, for every finite model string `class_name` and
every finite list of finite model strings `extensions`, the exact regenerated
submitted function terminates normally and returns:

- `class_name + "."` when the list is empty; or
- `class_name + "." + extensions[i]` for nonempty input, where `i` is the
  least index whose extension has maximal fixed-model score, and that score is
  the sum of `+1` for ASCII uppercase, `-1` for ASCII lowercase, and `0`
  otherwise.

This is a symbolic, unbounded finite-data theorem, not a finite enumeration or
bounded unrolling. The empty-list behavior is the candidate's defensible policy
for a case the docstring leaves open.

### Trust ledger

| Boundary | Accounting |
|---|---|
| Read-only supplied K semantics | Trusted benchmark model; candidate copy was recursively verified identical. |
| K parser/compiler, Haskell proof backend, SMT/KORE machinery, LLVM concrete backend, and host arithmetic/sequence builtins | Standard toolchain trust boundary; versions and fresh builds are recorded. |
| K constructor disjointness, subsort injection/projection, maps, sequences, and integer arithmetic | Ordinary fixed-model primitives used by both execution and proofs. |
| Proof-local projection simplifiers | Derived from the sole `Str ::= str(IntSeq)` constructor and confined by exact string guards. The positive connection is mechanically checked, but its trivial normalization makes the static derivation and rejected opposite probe part of the justification. This is a minor proof-local trust/evidence limitation, not an oracle. |
| Loop bridges | Not assumptions: each is preceded by a universal reachability connection proof against the lower-level definition. K's circular reachability reasoning is part of the trusted prover. |
| First-maximum interpretation of `bestCodes` | Formally computed by exhaustive strict-update/negated-update structural equations; its identification as “first maximum” additionally uses ordinary induction over a finite sequence. |
| CPython/source bridge | Supported by direct source inspection, trusted translation identity, directed tests, and 10,000 generated cases. Differential testing supports this bridge only; it does not replace the K theorem. |
| Unicode case behavior | Documented supplied-model gap. The fixed rules are ASCII-only; CPython and the submitted source are Unicode-aware. Witness: `("Gap", ["", "Ω"])` gives `"Gap."` in the fixed model and `"Gap.Ω"` in CPython. The candidate documents `Ω` and the model boundary in its trust ledger and introduces no further narrowing. |
| Empty extensions | Docstring-underdetermined. Candidate returns `class_name + "."`; canonical raises. The proof covers, rather than excludes, the candidate policy. |
| Unused opaque supplied symbols | Float, sort, hash, and other unused semantic families cannot occur in the exact submitted term and do not affect the target result. |

The Unicode discrepancy is model-versus-CPython, not
program-versus-docstring: the Python program uses the intended Python case
predicates and passes the concrete Unicode witness. Under campaign amendment
v2, that documented supplied-model gap requires the non-fatal
`CONCERNS / LEGIT` mapping.

VERDICT: CONCERNS
LEGITIMACY: LEGIT
